Trying to Conceive

hCG for men: selected uses, fertility and safety

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, is familiar as the hormone detected by pregnancy tests. It is also a prescription medicine with selected uses in men. Its suitability depends on the cause of a hormone problem, the exact product and fertility goals. Raising a blood testosterone result is not the same as improving sperm production, sexual symptoms or the chance of a baby.

One hormone, different products and approvals

hCG can imitate the action of luteinising hormone (LH). In the testes, LH normally signals Leydig cells to make testosterone. This can help when the hormonal signal is deficient and the testes can respond; it does not repair every cause of testicular failure.

Some products contain hCG purified from urine. Others contain recombinant choriogonadotropin alfa made using a cell line. For example, US PREGNYL has a selected male hypogonadotropic hypogonadism indication; US OVIDREL has female fertility indications. One product’s approval, route or allergy information cannot be applied to all others.

Low testosterone needs a diagnosis

Reduced sexual desire, fewer spontaneous erections, fatigue or changes in muscle and mood can have several causes. Symptoms alone, or one result below 300 ng/dL, do not establish which treatment is needed. Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms and consistently low testosterone, interpreted with an appropriate laboratory range.

A clinician usually confirms a low result with another morning fasting measurement and assesses the cause. LH and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) help distinguish a problem in the testes from deficient brain or pituitary signals. Other tests depend on the findings; hCG is not an automatic response to a single number.

When fertility treatment may include hCG

In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, inadequate LH and FSH signals can reduce testosterone and sperm production. A specialist may use hCG to replace the LH-like signal and monitor testosterone. FSH may then be added to support sperm production; these medicines do different jobs.

Selected infertile men with low testosterone may also be offered hormonal treatment after assessment. A high LH level suggesting primary testicular failure can mean a limited response. Hormone improvement does not guarantee sperm recovery, pregnancy or a live birth, and both partners’ circumstances matter.

Sexual function is a separate treatment goal

hCG may help symptoms in an appropriately selected hormone-deficient man, but it is not a general sexual-performance injection. Normal testosterone does not rule out erectile or libido problems, and injecting hCG is not a substitute for assessing them.

Erection, orgasm, desire and fertility are different functions. Medicines, vascular disease, sleep, stress and relationship factors may contribute to symptoms. Agree with the clinician which symptom is being treated and how benefit and adverse effects will be judged.

External testosterone and bodybuilding use

Testosterone supplied as a medicine or anabolic steroid can suppress the signals needed for sperm production, sometimes leading to no sperm in semen. Current AUA/ASRM guidance advises against prescribing external testosterone to men interested in current or future fertility. Recovery after stopping is variable and can be prolonged.

Adding hCG to testosterone has not been proven to protect every man’s fertility; the evidence is too limited for a general fertility-preservation recommendation. Do not start, combine or stop hormonal medicines, or use an online “post-cycle” regimen, on your own. Tell the specialist about all prescribed hormones, gym products and previous steroid use.

What the small studies can and cannot show

A 2005 study of 29 healthy men over three weeks measured testosterone inside the testes during external testosterone treatment. Maintaining that measurement with hCG was not proof of maintained sperm production or live birth. A 2013 retrospective series of 26 men reported semen findings during combined treatment, but lacked a randomised comparison.

A 2019 uncontrolled series of 20 selected men with symptoms and testosterone above 300 ng/dL reported some improvement. Such small, short or retrospective studies do not establish broad effectiveness, long-term safety or a sexual benefit for men with normal hormone results. Treatment decisions need the diagnosis and the stronger clinical guidance.

Check contraindications and the exact formulation

Before prescribing, the clinician checks the product label and medical history. The US PREGNYL label includes prior hypersensitivity to hCG or its ingredients, certain hormone-sensitive tumours including prostate cancer, hypothalamic or pituitary tumours and uncontrolled thyroid, adrenal or pituitary disorders among its contraindications.

Report heart or kidney disease, high blood pressure, fluid retention, migraine, asthma, epilepsy and all other medicines. Recombinant OVIDREL uses a Chinese hamster ovary cell line in manufacture; urine-derived hCG does not. A blanket “all hCG is hamster-derived” or hamster-allergy rule is inaccurate: a pharmacist must check the actual product and previous reactions.

Possible adverse effects and monitoring

Reported effects include injection-site reactions, headache, mood changes and tiredness; breast enlargement and fluid retention can occur in men. Report persistent swelling, new breast changes or troublesome symptoms. An adverse-effect list does not tell you how often each effect occurs in your situation.

Ovarian hyperstimulation warnings and women’s fertility-trial rates cannot be transferred directly to men. New abdominal pain, vomiting or other significant illness still needs assessment rather than being dismissed as a routine hormone effect. Review visits and blood tests, and semen tests when relevant, should be planned by the prescriber.

Know which symptoms need urgent help

If hCG hypersensitivity is suspected, stop using it and obtain medical advice before another dose. Throat or tongue swelling, serious breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness require emergency help immediately. Sudden facial or arm weakness or speech difficulty also needs emergency care even if it improves.

A new painful swollen leg needs urgent same-day assessment. Chest or upper-back pain, severe breathlessness, a very fast heartbeat or loss of consciousness require immediate emergency care; do not drive yourself. Sudden new breathlessness or coughing blood needs urgent assessment even without severe symptoms. These warnings do not mean blood clots are a common male hCG effect.

Use only an individual prescription and plan

Ask which indication the medicine treats, whether the use is approved locally or off-label, and what monitoring and follow-up are needed. Sperm response is assessed over time, not after a few injections, and alternative fertility approaches may be appropriate if treatment does not help.

Get training for the exact prescribed preparation, route, diluent and measuring device. Concentrations, units, storage after mixing and discard dates differ between products. Do not copy a dose from a study, swap preparations, share needles or inject a product of uncertain origin. Ask the pharmacist if instructions or storage are unclear.

hCG is not a weight-loss treatment

The FDA has not approved hCG for weight loss. Products advertised as hCG drops, sprays or pellets do not make a restrictive diet safe or reliably remove fat while preserving muscle. A prescription for a recognised hormone indication is not an endorsement of an hCG diet.

Plans promoting about 500 calories a day can cause serious problems including electrolyte disturbances, abnormal heart rhythms and gallstones. Do not follow an online hCG diet. Seek qualified help for weight concerns and tell a clinician about products and severe food restriction already being used.

Make the next decision with clear expectations

Bring previous hormone and semen results and a list of symptoms, medicines and fertility plans. Ask what diagnosis supports hCG, which changes would count as benefit, what side effects should prompt a call, and when the plan will be reviewed.

hCG can be useful for selected men, especially when a missing hormonal signal is the problem. It is not a universal cure for low testosterone, infertility or sexual concerns. A plan that weighs symptoms, reproductive goals and safety is more useful than pursuing a testosterone number alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the prescriber to explain the diagnosis, the exact product’s indication and the separate goals for symptoms and fertility.

Agree on hormone and, when relevant, semen follow-up; discuss fertility before using external testosterone and avoid unsupervised combinations.

Check preparation and storage with the pharmacist, keep the emergency warning plan accessible and avoid hCG weight-loss products.

How BeMama can help

A higher testosterone result does not prove improved fertility or sexual wellbeing. The useful questions are whether the diagnosis fits, whether the intended outcome improves and whether treatment remains safe.

When to seek help

Do not start or combine hormones or an hCG diet yourself. Suspected hypersensitivity means stop and seek medical advice before another dose. Airway swelling, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, sudden stroke signs, fainting or loss of consciousness need immediate emergency help; do not drive. A new painful swollen leg, sudden new breathlessness or coughing blood needs urgent assessment, with emergency care for severe symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • hCG provides an LH-like signal; it is not the same medicine or function as FSH.
  • Confirm low testosterone and its cause before choosing treatment; one number is not enough.
  • Neither hCG alone nor its addition to testosterone guarantees fertility or sexual benefit.
  • Use the exact prescribed formulation, monitoring and storage instructions; avoid bodybuilding regimens and hCG diets.
  • Get emergency help for serious allergy, stroke signs, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or loss of consciousness.

Frequently asked questions

Why might a man be prescribed hCG?

A specialist may prescribe it for selected hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or selected low-testosterone infertility after assessment. It stimulates an LH-like signal in the testes; it does not treat every cause of low testosterone or infertility.

What symptoms suggest testosterone deficiency?

Low desire, fewer spontaneous erections, fatigue or muscle and mood changes may be clues, but have other causes. Diagnosis needs symptoms plus consistently low properly timed testosterone measurements and an assessment of the cause.

Does hCG directly replace FSH?

No. Its main useful action is LH-like stimulation of Leydig-cell testosterone. FSH has a different role supporting sperm production and may be added by a specialist in selected conditions.

Can I preserve fertility by taking hCG with testosterone?

It is not guaranteed. Small studies are insufficient to recommend that combination as a general fertility-preservation strategy. Discuss current or future fertility before external testosterone is prescribed; do not build your own hormone regimen.

Will it improve sex if my testosterone is normal?

There is no established general benefit. Small uncontrolled studies do not prove effectiveness or long-term safety for that purpose. Erectile, desire or orgasm problems need their own assessment.

Is all hCG made using hamster cells?

No. Some hCG is urine-derived; recombinant choriogonadotropin alfa uses a cell line in manufacture. Indications, ingredients, routes and allergy precautions are product-specific, so check the exact medicine with a pharmacist.

What side effects or warning signs matter?

Local reactions, headache, mood symptoms, breast enlargement or fluid retention may need review. Suspected allergy means stop and seek advice before another dose; airway swelling, serious breathing difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness require emergency help. A painful swollen leg needs urgent same-day assessment; chest pain or severe breathlessness needs emergency care. Do not drive yourself in an emergency.

Can hCG be used for weight loss?

It is not FDA-approved for weight loss. hCG products do not protect against the dangers of extreme calorie restriction, including electrolyte disturbance and abnormal heart rhythms. Do not use an online hCG diet or unverified injections.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
